It's not glass quality, it's the correction of chromatic and geometric aberrations. The transmission curves at Edmunds shows optical glasses are nearly identical, except in the uv and infrared. You are contradicting yourself. What makes a difference in index refraction, flint and crown glass is the quality of the glass. And the better the glad material the better the glass quality. The charts in the link make it pretty obvious.

Flint and crown glass isn't quality, it's dispersion. And dispersion corrects chromatic aberrations. The primary aberrations, astigmatism, tilt, defocus, spherical aberration, distortion, and field curvature are products of the shape of the lens alone. Quality optics corrects aberrations by adding lenses which makes them more expensive. Nowhere in any optical ray tracing calculations is there a quality variable. It's a made up term. I am an optical engineer.

All terms are made up terms. But you are saying the material the glass is made from and the quality of that glass makes no difference? That is good to hear from an optical engineer. Not sure how to explain the weird distortions I have seen in glass. Must have been something other than the quality and that old glass they used to use in the old days where you couldn't really see through it very well was do to something other than the optical quality of that glass any glass is good glass and slag glass should no longer be thrown away and instead be used for optics.

The distortions are those aberrations I was talking about. The easiest shape to make a lens is spherical, and the radius of curvature causes aberrations. This is due to Snell's law which simply describes how the direction of light changes at the interface of glass and air and is only dependent on the index of refraction. This is true whether the glass is a beer bottle or the most exotic glass. Any optically clear glass is going to transmit 99% of light. But let's say glass quality is a thing for a moment and say poor quality glass transmits 90% of light. What else could change? Nothing. Snell's law would still apply so radius of curvature would still cause aberrations. What would be the result of low quality glass ? A slightly dimmer image. Glass is mostly silica, and the additional chemicals change physical properties like strength, thermal expansion, index or refraction, and dispersion. Dispersion is how different the index of refraction is for blue and red light, meaning a fat or skinny rainbow made from a piece of glass. The last thing is the sharpness of an image determined by the diameter of the first lens of the system ( objective) and to fairly compare optics the objectives should be the same size. Try out the cheaper optics, some are as good or better than the most expensive.
Coatings are bs? I don’t have expensive scopes, can’t afford them.

Coatings don't improve image quality. Coatings are used to decrease the light reflected at the surface of the glass. Uncoated glass looses on average 4% light at each surface. If there's a large number of elements, image brightness can be dimmed noticeably. But coatings to decrease the loss to 1% starts to get expensive, and aren't necessary in most cases. Your not gaining much, since you are getting a bump in brightness by focusing an image.

But, not to be a dick, - what I am saying here is just kind of a community service announcement - guys should not make the mistake that many guys make of thinking that there is a big overlap between boxing/martial arts and self defense. It is of course basic to be able to hit and move and cover well, but that is just basics.

If we want to prepare for self defense, we have to understand what a self defense situation really is and that it differs greatly from sportsfighting situations.

Here are my Four General Principles for Defining a Self Defense Situation:

  1. One of the participants must be unwilling or unwitting. By unwitting I mean, I may go out to the carpark to fight some guy, thinking it is going to be a "fair fight" but I am foolish in thinking that, because I will probably be jumped, especially if I start to win.

  2. A self defense situation is always unfair: big on small, skilled on unskilled, young on old, fast on slow, many on one, and so on.

  3. A self defense situation most often involves an escalation and an initial entry (these do not occur in sportsfighting). It is usually not possible to "block" or react well/successfully to an initial entry - because "Actor beats Reactor" - so we need to be able to recognize escalations (intimidation) early and preempt the aggressor's initial entry. That is a very big psycho-social issue in self defense because self defense is "boarding house rules", - "first in, best fed".

  4. Self defense situations can very easily lead to death or severe injury, inadvertently or otherwise, when you fall and hit your head on the ground, or get kicked in the head by the opponent's friend, and so on. So self defense situations are deadly serious, even if on the face of things they may not look so dangerous.
